one_liner: coost v3's fastream (append-only text buffer) and fastring (heap string), claimed 10-30x faster than snprintf with no published harness.
what_it_does: fastream is a move-only byte buffer with operator<< and a variadic cat() for building text, meant to replace std::ostringstream and snprintf-based concatenation; fastring is a std::string-like class on the same {capacity, size, pointer} buffer with find/rfind/trim/replace/split helpers and operator<<. Both live in coost v3 (headers co/fastream.h and co/fastring.h, last released in v3.0.2, 2023-11-23); coost v4.0.0 removed them and folded the design into co::string in co/string.h. Neither is a drop-in: fastring has no iterators, insert or erase, and fastream has no manipulators or format strings.
how_it_is_fast: There is no locale, no virtual streambuf and no format-string parsing: operator<< appends straight into a contiguous buffer that grows by 1.5x through co::realloc, which can extend a block in place inside coost's thread-local slab allocator (blocks up to 2048 bytes in 16-byte units, sized free). Integers go through a 10,000-entry table of pre-rendered 4-digit ASCII groups whose first byte also encodes the digit count, so a 64-bit value needs at most four divide-by-10000 steps and five table loads; pointers and hex use a 256-entry byte-to-two-hex-digits table; doubles use Milo Yip's Grisu2 dtoa (the RapidJSON one). fastring::find uses memchr for the first byte and then Eric Blake's Two-Way substring search.
when_to_use: Maintaining code already on coost v3 (its log, json and flag modules use fastream/fastring internally) where switching to std::ostringstream would add overhead.
Hot paths that concatenate integers, pointers, booleans and short strings into a reusable buffer (log lines, keys, protocol text) and can tolerate shortest-or-truncated float output.
Builds limited to C++11 (gcc 4.8+, clang 3.3+, VS2015+) that still want allocation-light string building without pulling in {fmt}.
Single-threaded or thread-local buffers that are cleared and reused, so the 1.5x growth and in-place realloc amortise to near-zero allocations.
when_not_to_use: New code: fastring.h and fastream.h no longer exist after coost v4.0.0 (2026-09-15); use co::string from v4, or {fmt}/std::to_chars outside coost.

Many small, short-lived strings: fastring has no small-string optimization (issue #282, closed in May 2025 without SSO; v4 co::string keeps the same three-field layout), so every non-empty string is a heap allocation where std::string would use its inline buffer.

Output that must match printf or iostream formatting: fastream << double prints at most 6 decimal places by truncation, not rounding (issue #333: dp::_n(3.14159265, 4) prints 3.1415; maintainer: rounding is not considered), and there is no width, padding, precision or hex manipulator.
Generic code that expects a std::string-shaped type: no begin()/end() iterators, no insert/erase/at, no allocator template parameter, char only.
Projects that want a standalone header: both classes need coost's compiled fast.cc, fastring.cc and mem.cc and its global allocator.

integration.form: static lib (libco from coost v3.0.2; xmake or CMake, also vcpkg and conan); v4 replaces it with co::string
integration.dependencies: coost core: fast.h/fast.cc (integer and hex tables, Grisu2 dtoa), mem.h/mem.cc (co::alloc thread-local allocator), god.h, murmur hash for std::hash<fastring>, fastring.cc (memmem, trim, replace)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (README: gcc 4.8+, clang 3.3+, Visual Studio 2015+); default xmake builds use -O2 ("faster"), benchmark targets -O3
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows (CI badges for all three in v3.0.2); 32- and 64-bit
integration.thread_safety: Same as std::string: no shared state between copies (reference counting was removed in July 2020 after issue #59); concurrent mutation of one object needs external locking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — fastream covers ostringstream's operator<< for built-in types but is move-only and has no manipulators or locale; fastring mirrors much of std::string's search and compare API but lacks iterators, insert/erase, SSO and allocator customization

gotchas: Harness flaw: no code backs the '10~30 times faster than snprintf' sentence. The only snprintf comparison in the repo (v3.0.2 test/fast.cc) times the bare u64toa/u64toh/dtoa primitives, not fastream; its default range 1000..9999 keeps every integer at four digits, so u64toa only ever takes its single-table-lookup branch, and dtoa (shortest round-trip, Grisu2) is timed against snprintf("%.7g") on the single value 3.14159, i.e. different output contracts. No results are published.

Harness flaw in the fastring-vs-std::string code (v3.0.2 test/str.cc): the 'ss = ss.c_str() + 1' case starts from an 8,191-character string, but co's benchmark macro runs one warm-up call and then 100,000 iterations for any body under 1 microsecond, so after 8,191 iterations both strings are empty and over 90% of the timed iterations assign an empty string; the harness also times a single batch with no repetition and BM_use is an empty out-of-line call placed after the timed loop. master benchmark/string.cc (co::string) has the same shape and also publishes nothing.
append(uint16), append(uint32) and append(uint64) on fastream/fastring append the raw binary bytes, not decimal text; use operator<< or cat() for text.

fast::i32toa/i64toa negate the value before converting, which is signed-overflow undefined behaviour for INT32_MIN/INT64_MIN (works on common two's-complement builds, but not guaranteed under optimisation).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when you are already inside coost v3; for formatting numbers into fixed buffers to_static_string (std::to_chars-based, with published numbers) or MengRao/str are cleaner standalone choices, and for a faster std::string replacement EASTL string or FastString publish actual measurements against std::string while fastring publishes none and lacks SSO.
verified_claims_summary: The only number is a first-party docs sentence (coost v3 docs, archived at coostdocs commit deb7584; the Chinese page says it was measured) that fastream is about 10-30x faster than snprintf across platforms and that std::ostringstream is several times slower than snprintf; no workload, compiler, flags, CPU or table accompanies it and no harness in any branch times fastream itself. fastring against std::string has benchmark code (v3.0.2 test/str.cc, master benchmark/string.cc) with no published results, and the code has the degenerate-input flaw noted above.
status_note: coost is actively maintained (MIT, last commit 2026-09-28, tag v4.0.1), but fastream and fastring themselves are retired: they exist only up to tag v3.0.2 and their successor co::string has no performance claim, so treat this entry as historical and vendorable only together with coost's allocator and number-conversion code.
